source: Stab and Gurevych (2017) Recognizing Insufficiently Supported Arguments in Argumentative Essays
finding: Founding corpus for the S criterion. 1,029 student-essay arguments labelled sufficient or insufficient. Three expert annotators reached substantial but not perfect agreement.
numbers: 433 arguments double-annotated by 3 annotators: observed agreement 91.07%, Fleiss kappa .7672, Krippendorff alpha .7673. Class split: 681 sufficient (66.2%), 348 insufficient (33.8%).
limits: Student essays only. Annotators overlooked modal verbs ('can' needs only one example) and read longer arguments as more sufficient. Quantifiers like 'some', 'various' caused disagreement.
agent_relevance: Sufficiency is judgeable at alpha about .77 on one genre, but known human biases (length, modal verbs) mean our S8 sufficiency check should state the claim strength (can/most/all) before counting support.

source: Stab and Gurevych (2017) Recognizing Insufficiently Supported Arguments in Argumentative Essays
finding: Supervised models detect insufficient arguments close to human level on this corpus. A CNN reached 92.5% of the human upper bound in accuracy.
numbers: Human upper bound accuracy .911, macro F1 .887. CNN accuracy .843, macro F1 .827 (F1 insufficient .770). SVM with manual features accuracy .798, macro F1 .770. Named entities alone: macro F1 .681; syntax alone: .640. Majority baseline macro F1 .398.
limits: In-genre, in-corpus, cross-validation. Features such as named entities and length are cues, not a test of whether support truly suffices.
agent_relevance: Surface cues predict labels well. A checker built on cues would pass the benchmark and still not test real sufficiency.

source: Gurcke, Alshomary and Wachsmuth (2021) Assessing the Sufficiency of Arguments through Conclusion Generation
finding: Tested the idea that a sufficient argument lets you generate its conclusion from the premises. Generation helped little. A RoBERTa classifier on premises alone matched the full-input model, so the benchmark does not require the conclusion at all.
numbers: Human upper bound macro F1 .883 (accuracy .911). CNN .831. RoBERTa all inputs: acc .896, macro F1 .885. RoBERTa premises-only: acc .887, F1 .875. Conclusion-only: acc .641, F1 .553. Generated-conclusion-only: F1 .532. 20 x 5-fold CV.
limits: Same Stab and Gurevych corpus. Authors note many different conclusions can follow from the same premises, so generation is not unique.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence of a shortcut: premises alone predict the 'sufficient' label. Benchmark scores on sufficiency do not show the model checks premises against the conclusion.

source: Liu, Feng and Chang (2024) CASA: Causality-driven Argument Sufficiency Assessment
finding: Zero-shot method that asks an LLM to imagine situations where the premise holds but the conclusion fails (a counterfactual objection), then checks with NLI. Beat plain zero-shot and one-shot prompting of 7B models on two fallacy sets, but absolute accuracy stays modest.
numbers: BIG-bench logical fallacy set: CASA (LLaMA-2-7B) acc 79.0, macro-F1 73.4; zero-shot LLaMA-2 70.0/66.8; one-shot 74.1/68.6; TULU zero-shot 59.5/59.3. Climate fallacy set: CASA LLaMA-2 67.9/61.2; zero-shot LLaMA-2 51.9/48.0; TULU zero-shot 33.0/30.3.
limits: Only 7B models, no GPT-4-class judge (authors worry about BIG-bench contamination). Small test sets (Climate has 30 correct and 76 fallacious).
agent_relevance: A sufficiency check that searches for the missing support (an objection case) beats a bare 'is this sufficient?' question. Fits G2/G3: look for a concrete failing case, do not opine.

source: Liu, Feng and Chang (2024) CASA: Causality-driven Argument Sufficiency Assessment
finding: Human check of using CASA objections to repair essays. Annotators judged CASA objections more rational and feasible than directly prompted ones, and revisions based on them improved sufficiency more often than they harmed it.
numbers: 100 sampled essay arguments, 3 annotators each. Rationality / feasibility: prompting TULU 84% / 60%, LLaMA-2 90% / 67%; CASA TULU 90% / 76%, LLaMA-2 92% / 81%. Revised-better vs original-better: prompting LLaMA-2 51% vs 23% (26% tie); CASA LLaMA-2 58% vs 7% (35% tie). Revisions written by GPT-4.
limits: Annotators' own sufficiency judgments are low-agreement (see b06). Only a sample of 100.
agent_relevance: Objection-then-revise improves sufficiency in judged outputs. Supports a Verify step that names one missing premise and lets the answer be revised once.

source: Liu, Feng and Chang (2024) CASA: Causality-driven Argument Sufficiency Assessment (footnote on the AAE corpus)
finding: Re-examines the Stab and Gurevych sufficiency labels. Overall agreement looks high, but agreement collapses on the cases that matter. Authors dropped the labels and kept only the essays.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha .77 overall, but only .14 on the 32% of instances that at least one annotator marked insufficient.
limits: Footnote-level reanalysis, authors' own computation as reported.
agent_relevance: The headline alpha of .77 hides that 'insufficient' is the contested label. An agent should not treat a binary sufficient flag as ground truth; give it as a graded call with a named gap.

source: Mirzakhmedova, Gohsen, Chang, Stein (2024) Are Large Language Models Reliable Argument Quality Annotators?
finding: GPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 rated 320 arguments on the 15-dimension Wachsmuth taxonomy (which includes local acceptability, relevance, sufficiency). Models are far more self-consistent than humans, but agreement with humans is only moderate, and worst on sufficiency.
numbers: Within-group Krippendorff alpha for local acceptability/relevance/sufficiency: human novices .43/.36/.35, human experts .33/.41/.27; GPT-3 .64-.79 across prompts; PaLM 2 .60-.78; one GPT-3 variant .97-.98. Human-LLM alpha on unanimous human subsets: PaLM 2 up to .71 (appropriateness, global relevance); systematic disagreement for GPT-3 vs experts on local and global sufficiency. 108 student novices, 10 arguments each.
quote: The results reveal that LLMs exhibit greater consistency in evaluating argument quality compared to both novice and expert human annotators
limits: GPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 only (GPT-4 not used for cost). PaLM 2 refused 23% of items on content policy. High LLM self-agreement is not validity: the same prompt gives the same answer.
agent_relevance: Sufficiency is the dimension where a model judge fails to track humans. Do not let the model grade its own S8 sufficiency check without an independent test.

source: Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024) Are Large Language Models Reliable Argument Quality Annotators?
finding: Adding model ratings to human ratings changes agreement depending on the model. PaLM 2 raised group agreement significantly, GPT-3 lowered it.
numbers: Human experts baseline alpha .40. Adding 3 PaLM 2 annotations: .44; adding 5: .50. Adding 5 GPT-3 annotations: .37 (adding 1: .32, a drop). Novices baseline .37; +5 PaLM 2 .43-.45.
limits: Significance marks in the original table were lost in extraction; the direction is stated in the paper text.
agent_relevance: A weaker or misaligned model as extra judge hurts. Extra judges help only if they bring independent signal, consistent with G4 (samples from one model are not independent).

source: Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024) Are Large Language Models Reliable Argument Quality Annotators? (prompt and variance results)
finding: Prompt wording matters and the effect is model-specific. Expert definitions raised GPT-3 agreement with expert humans, novice definitions with novices. Reasoning-before-rating prompts did not give a uniform gain. Agreement with humans swings widely by dimension.
numbers: Agreement ranges across prompts: credibility [0.08, 0.62], appropriateness [0.06, 0.71]; sufficiency varied even more. Four prompt types (novice/expert, with and without reasoning), three runs each.
limits: Only two models. Ranges read from a figure caption and text, not a full table.
agent_relevance: Definition of the criterion in the prompt shifts the verdict. If S8 uses the ARS criteria it must pin the exact wording and test it on held-out cases.

source: Dhole, Shu, Agichtein (2024) ConQRet: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Argumentation with LLM Judges
finding: A GPT-4o judge that scores all 15 Wachsmuth dimensions in one listwise prompt reached agreement with experts on ArgQuality (320 arguments) at about human level for overall quality. Self-consistency over three runs raised it further.
numbers: Per-dimension alpha for GPT-4o judges mostly .2 to .57 (local sufficiency listwise runs about .37 to .55; global acceptability about .54-.56; global sufficiency about .40-.47). Overall quality alpha .43 in one pointwise baseline vs about .41-.48 listwise. Averages across dimensions ~.45-.52 zero-shot.
limits: Table layout in the PDF text is garbled, so single cell values are uncertain; ranges are read from tables 5, 13, 14. Compared to different baselines than b07.
agent_relevance: Even a frontier judge with all definitions in the prompt lands in the .3-.55 band on sufficiency and relevance. Treat S8 verdicts as a hint that needs a code-checked partner.

source: Dhole et al. (2024) ConQRet
finding: Order of the 15 dimensions in the prompt changes the scores a lot. Averaging three orderings plus self-consistency stabilised results. Zero-shot beat few-shot.
numbers: Listwise runs with three dimension orders gave clearly different per-dimension alpha (e.g. local relevance .203 vs .447 for different runs in Table 13/14). Pooling the three runs raised agreement 'only at the expense of 2 additional inference calls'. Zero-shot more effective than 5-shot.
limits: Single model family (GPT-4o), one corpus.
agent_relevance: Order effects in rubric prompts are real. A checklist should be run in fixed and shuffled order and compared (a counted step, not a judged one).

source: Dhole et al. (2024) ConQRet (retrieval and irrelevant context tests)
finding: Tests whether LLM judges notice irrelevant evidence (the R in ARS). Fine-grained per-document relevance scores fall monotonically as irrelevant documents are swapped in, while single holistic scores do not reliably fall. Weaker 7B and 14B models failed to follow the evaluation format.
numbers: Fine-grained context-relevance metrics decreased monotonically with rising irrelevant context; single-score metrics did not consistently decrease (Tables 15-17). GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-70B and Gemini-1.5-Flash showed the needed sensitivity; phi-3 small and medium did not.
limits: Synthetic replacement of retrieved documents, oracle setting.
agent_relevance: Judge relevance per piece of evidence, not once for the whole answer. Per-item relevance checks detect injected irrelevant material; one overall score does not.

source: Deshpande, Sourati, Ilievski, Morstatter (2023/2024) Contextualizing Argument Quality Assessment with Relevant Knowledge (SPARK)
finding: Adding LLM-generated context (feedback, hidden assumptions, a counter-argument, a similar-quality argument) to a dual-BERT scorer improved prediction of cogency, effectiveness and reasonableness. Feedback and assumptions helped cogency and reasonableness most.
numbers: Spearman gain over BERT baseline 0.08 to 0.17 across three metrics; effectiveness +61%. Human rating of augmentations on 1-5 scale (50 items): assumptions validity 4.95, counter-arguments 4.93, feedback 4.87; informativeness feedback 3.80, assumptions 4.91, counter-arguments 4.94.
limits: GPT-3.5 generated augmentations, BERT scorer trained on regression labels. Feedback best out of domain. Humans rated feedback less informative than the model benefited from.
agent_relevance: Surfacing unstated assumptions and a counter-argument improves quality prediction, supporting a Verify step that lists hidden premises and the best objection.

source: Romberg, Maurer, Wachsmuth, Lapesa (2025) Towards a perspectivist turn in argument quality assessment
finding: Survey of about 100 argument-quality papers and 24 datasets with annotator-level labels. Experts agree most, yet only weakly. Models trained on one annotator group do not transfer to another, so a single gold score hides real perspective differences.
numbers: Dagstuhl-ArgQuality Krippendorff alpha cogency: experts .372, crowd .230, novice .099-.107 in several group readings; mixed expert+novice+crowd .083. GAQ: experts .175, crowd .156, expert+crowd .142. Overall-quality alpha experts .443 vs mixed .115 (Dagstuhl). Transfer experts to crowd MAE .43-.53 vs expert to novice .60-.70. Categorisation reliability across authors: Fleiss kappa 1.0 for logical cogency, mean .52 over 23 categories. 45 datasets gave no annotator info; fewer than 20% recruited by diverse selection.
limits: Authors' pilot analysis on two corpora. English is over 85% of datasets, so cultural variation is largely unmeasured.
agent_relevance: Acceptability depends on who the audience is. For open answers state the audience and the premises assumed, instead of claiming one correct acceptability score.

source: Ocampo, Nyiranziza, Ceolin (2026) Argument Quality Assessment with Large Language Models: A Pairwise Bradley-Terry Approach
finding: 12 open-weight LLMs, three prompt styles, pairwise judging on Webis-ArgQuality-20 (13,952 comparisons) across logic, rhetoric and dialectic, where logic includes local acceptability, relevance and sufficiency. The best model reaches only moderate agreement with humans.
numbers: Llama-70B few-shot: Pearson .474/.469/.476 and Kendall .329/.318/.333 across dimensions (logic, rhetoric, dialectic); Cohen kappa .493; agreement 53.0%. Majority baseline Pearson .07-.13; random about 0. Second best Qwen2.5-72B zero-shot Pearson .463. Olmo2-7B and Mistral-22B correlations near or below zero. Labels differ across three runs in at most 7.75% of cases.
limits: Open-weight models only, no GPT-4-class or reasoning model. Pairwise setup with ties. Stability is not validity.
agent_relevance: Best open models give r about .47 with human pairwise quality. Useful for ranking, not for an accept/reject verdict; ranking two candidate answers is easier than scoring one.

source: Ocampo et al. (2026) Pairwise Bradley-Terry approach (position and bias findings)
finding: Small models show a position preference and rarely say tie, while larger models predict fewer ties. Models disagree with each other in complementary ways, so combining models can beat the single best one.
numbers: Ground truth comparisons: B preferred in about 40%, A 41-44%, tie 14-18%. Few-shot prompting raised tie use to 62.97% for some models; stronger models predicted fewer ties. Krippendorff alpha across runs: some models .39 to .63, most near-perfect.
limits: Details for specific models are in appendix tables not fully read.
agent_relevance: Run pairwise judgments in both orders and count a flip as a no-signal. Cheap, code-checked, and in line with G4.

source: Sternlicht, Gera, Bar-Haim, Hope, Slonim (2025) Debatable Intelligence: Benchmarking LLM Judges via Debate Speech Evaluation
finding: Over 600 debate speeches, 15 human raters per speech, 5-point agree rating. Large LLM judges can match individual humans, but they rate speeches lower and their score distributions differ from human ones even when rankings agree.
numbers: Models above about 7B generally better; Qwen-2.5-72B exceeds human-human pairwise kappa. Strong judges defined as Kendall tau-C above 0.5 against average of 15 humans. Some frontier models (o3) underperform. Chain-of-thought helped most larger judges slightly and hurt some small ones. Llama-3.1-8B had higher kappa but lower tau than Llama-3.1-70B.
limits: One 5-point holistic question, speeches about 600 words. Relevance and strength are folded into one score, so no ARS-specific number.
agent_relevance: Judges that rank well can still be miscalibrated in level. Use them for relative comparison, not absolute thresholds.

source: Svedholm-Hakkinen, Hietanen, Baron (2024) Individual Differences in Argument Strength Discrimination
finding: Preregistered study, N=278 after exclusions, 40 strong/weak argument pairs from consequence, analogy, symptom and authority schemes, rated for strength. People tell weak from strong largely like experts do, but rate strong arguments too low. Discrimination looked like one ability across schemes.
numbers: Strong minus weak difference 1.30 points (SD 0.35) for participants vs 1.61 for experts. Mean strong rating +0.19, weak -1.11 on -2 to +2. 90% of weak arguments rated below midpoint, only 63% of strong arguments above. Correlation of participants with expert panel across 80 arguments r=.62. Expert ICC .62 overall (.58 to .64 by scheme). Reliability omega .71.
limits: Finnish general population, online. Participants started with 343, 65 excluded. Strength rated as one global judgment rather than separate A, R, S.
agent_relevance: Weak arguments are caught; good ones are under-credited. A Verify step tuned only to find flaws will over-reject sound answers.

source: Svedholm-Hakkinen, Hietanen, Baron (2024) Individual Differences in Argument Strength Discrimination
finding: Moderators. Analytic thinking dispositions predict discrimination moderately. Intuitive style, self-rated effort and prior argument-analysis familiarity do not. Overconfidence slightly hurts.
numbers: Observed correlations with discrimination: Need for Cognition .301, CRT .297, Actively Open-Minded Thinking .314, Intellectual Humility .255, education .182, overconfidence -.147, intuition .001, mental effort -.049, age .099. Disattenuated betas AOT .18, NFC .17, CRT .18, CIHS .15; multiple R2 .19 (R .44). Familiarity with argument analysis: no relation (most reported none or little).
limits: Correlational. Overconfidence is computed from CRT accuracy, so it overlaps with CRT. Mental effort was one self-report item.
agent_relevance: Effort alone does not improve argument evaluation; dispositions toward open-minded checking do. Supports triggering checks on a signal rather than by adding thinking time.

source: Svedholm-Hakkinen et al. (2024) (think-aloud background section)
finding: Summarises that laypeople thinking aloud about arguments raise mostly relevance and appropriateness of the argument to the claim. Skilled arguers separate from unskilled ones by judging how the argument relates to the claim.
numbers: No new numbers; cites the Johnson and Blair (1977) relevance, acceptability and sufficiency triad as the normative base.
limits: Secondary summary of other studies, not re-verified here.
agent_relevance: Relevance is the criterion people already apply by instinct. Sufficiency and acceptability are the ones to prompt for explicitly.

source: Johnson and Blair (1977) Logical Self-Defense; Govier (1985) A Practical Study of Argument
finding: Founding statements of the RAS or ARS criteria: premises must be acceptable, relevant to the conclusion and jointly sufficient. Replace deductive validity as the general test for informal arguments. Seen in a search snippet only; the book text was not opened this session.
numbers: No empirical numbers. Wachsmuth et al. (2017) later split these into local acceptability, relevance, sufficiency within cogency.
limits: Normative theory, no experimental test of whether following the criteria makes people judge better.
agent_relevance: Source for the three-question S8 checklist. No evidence from these books that the checklist improves outcomes; effect has to be measured on our agent.

source: Hoffmann and Catrambone (2023) criteria for objectively bad arguments, Informal Logic 43(1)
finding: Proposes eight criteria for identifying objectively bad arguments, going beyond ARS, and argues students should learn them. Known only from a search snippet; the PDF would not download.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Not opened. The abstract-level claim is all that is available.
agent_relevance: A candidate extension of the ARS list. Fetch the full text before using any of its eight criteria.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007) The rationality of informal argumentation: a Bayesian approach to reasoning fallacies, Psychological Review
finding: Rival to the checklist view: argument strength is graded and depends on content, so the same form can be strong or weak (a drug declared safe after no toxic effects were seen vs ghosts exist because no one disproved them). Epistemic closure, meaning how thoroughly one searched, drives sufficiency. Search snippet only.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: Full text did not download. Experimental N and effect sizes not seen.
agent_relevance: Sufficiency is graded and tied to how much was searched. S8 could ask how complete the check was, not only whether support exists.

source: Wachsmuth and colleagues (2024) Argument Quality Assessment in the Age of Instruction-Following Large Language Models (LREC-COLING position paper)
finding: Position paper: instruction-following LLMs could make argument quality assessment more reliable, but should be taught argumentation theory and not tuned only for leaderboards. Known from search snippets and from how b07, b10 and b15 cite it.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports building theory-grounded criteria (ARS) into the prompt rather than asking for a generic quality score.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017) taxonomy of argument quality as reproduced in Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024) Table 1 and Romberg et al. (2025) Appendix D
finding: The taxonomy nests ARS twice: locally (cogency: are the premises acceptable, relevant, sufficient) and globally (reasonableness: does the argument as a whole resolve the issue, is it relevant to agreement, does it rebut counter-arguments). Global sufficiency is defined as rebutting counter-arguments, a different thing from local sufficiency.
numbers: 15 dimensions in total; cogency 3 sub-dimensions, effectiveness 5, reasonableness 3, plus overall quality. ArgQuality corpus 320 arguments.
limits: Definitions as quoted by secondary papers, not read in the 2017 original.
agent_relevance: For an open answer the useful split is local ARS on each premise plus a global check that the strongest counter-argument was answered.

source: Cross-paper pattern: sufficiency is the weakest ARS dimension for humans and models (b01, b06, b07, b10)
finding: Across five measurements sufficiency has the lowest or most unstable agreement of the three ARS dimensions. Human experts: local sufficiency alpha .27 vs relevance .41. GPT-3 vs experts: systematic disagreement on sufficiency. Insufficiency labels: alpha .14 among cases flagged by any annotator.
numbers: Mirzakhmedova: human novice local sufficiency .35, expert .27; global sufficiency expert .17. CASA footnote: .14 on contested items. ConQRet GPT-4o sufficiency alpha about .37-.55.
limits: Synthesis by this agent across different corpora and metrics, not a single meta-analysis. No published meta-analysis of ARS reliability was found.
agent_relevance: Weight S8 findings on sufficiency lowest and make them need a concrete missing-evidence statement before they trigger a revision.

source: Gap statement (no source): direct tests of ARS training or prompts on answer quality
finding: No study found in this search that gives an LLM the Johnson and Blair ARS checklist as a verification step and measures end-task accuracy or quality change. The nearest results are CASA (sufficiency by objection), SPARK (assumption and counter-argument context) and fine-grained judges (ConQRet). Based on 6 searches and arXiv/Semantic Scholar queries that were rate limited.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence of evidence after limited search. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API returned rate-limit errors.
agent_relevance: The ARS checklist for S8 would be our own test (an [O] item). Plan a held-out A/B with and without it.
